9.7.8 Count Vector vs. Count Vector with Stemming and Lemmatization vs. TF-IDF Vector

Count vector, Count vector with Stemming, and Lemmatization and TF-IDF Vector are three different ways to create word embeddings in a BoW model. These three ways to measure the importance of a word finally help create a word vector for a document. The ranking of the word within the document changes based on the measure selected. Let us deep dive into the tweets from user ‘PIBImphal. For PIBImphal, the count of words in twitter_word_count, twitter word stem count and twitter word tf count is 551. For the PIBImphal, let us compare Tables 9.30 and 9.31:

1. Table 9.30 without stemming and lemmatization shows ‘church’ and ‘urges’ as two words in the first six records sorted by ‘n’.

2. Table 9.31 with stemming and lemmatization shows ‘appeal’ and ‘minist’ as two words in the first six records sorted by ‘n’.

The stemming and lemmatization process brought words

1. ‘appeals’ and ‘appealed’ in their root form ‘appeal’ and thus increased the count of the word ‘appeal’.

2. ‘minister’ and ‘ministers’ in their root form ‘minist’, thus showing a count of eight.

This resulted in knocking off the last two records from Table 9.30 and offered a clear indication of how word ordering may get changed due to stemming and lemmatization.

The use of TF-IDF helps extract words which are characteristics of a particular user (screenName) within a collection of users who tweeted on the same topic. To validate the statement, let us compare Tables 9.30 and 9.32:

1. Table 9.30 without stemming and lemmatization shows ‘follow’ and ‘peopl’ as two words in the first seven records sorted by ‘n’.

2. Table 9.32 with stemming and lemmatization plus TF-IDF shows ‘church’ and ‘pastor’ as two words in the first seven records sorted by ‘n’.

Based on TF-IDF, we can see words like ‘church’ and ‘pastor’ in Table 9.32 which is much more relevant in tweets from PIBImphal, compared to words like ‘follow’ and ‘people’ which may have been used by many users in the corpus. In Table 9.30, ‘follow’ with a count of13 could not make it to the top seven records in Table 9.32. At the same time, ‘pastor’ with just six counts was ranked higher than minist in Table 9.32 (table sorted in ascending order of TF-IDF).

The BoW has its own shortcomings but is a useful way for visualization of textual data. The BoW model can also help build basic prediction-based models (discussed in later sections). However, let us continue with the last query on the twitter data.

9.8 | Sentiment Analysis

After having created the BoW model and with the understanding of basic word embed-dings, let us delve into the other topic which is of interest in text analytics. Sentiment of the users regarding a particular topic is of great interest. In this case, we want to know the emotions of the users on topics related to COVID-19. Through human intelligence, one can read through the tweets and get an understanding of the emotion reflected by the user. It could be a positive/negative tweet or a happy/neutral/sad tweet, etc. But it will be overwhelming for a human being to read through all the tweets and tag the tweets to reflect emotional intent.

Tidytext comes with inbuilt lexicon (available through textdata package) which can help categorize the tweet into one of the predefined tags of emotion. Four general-purpose lexicons in tidytext are as follows:

1. Afinn – This lexicon from Finn Årup Nielsen (Nielsen, 2011) categorizes 2,477 unique unigrams on a score of −5 (negative sentiment) to 5 (positive sentiment). This is licensed under Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0. Table 9.37 shows six observations from afinn lexicon.

Word sentiment

1. Nrc – This lexicon from Saif Mohammad and Peter Turney (2013) categorizes words under the labels ‘trust’, ‘fear’, ‘negative’, ‘sadness’, ‘anger’, ‘surprise’, ‘positive’, ‘disgust’, ‘joy’, and ‘anticipation’. It is by far the most comprehensive, having categorized 6,468 unigrams under these labels. A word can have a mapping to more than one label. This dataset requires license for commercial use. Table 9.38 shows six observations from nrc lexicon.

2. Bing – This lexicon from Bing Liu (2015) and collaborators categorizes words in binary fashion, that is, positive/negative, that is, two unique labels. It has categorized 6,783 unigrams under these labels. By default, only this lexicon is available as a part of the tidytext. Table 9.39 shows six observations from bing lexicon (S Biguzzi, 2020).

3. lougharn – This lexicon from Loughran-McDonald (2019) categorizes words under the labels ‘negative’, ‘positive’, ‘uncertainty’, ‘litigious’, ‘constraining’, and ‘superfluous’. The lexicon has categorized 3,917 English words under these emotional intents. Words may have a mapping under more than one label. This lexicon requires license for commercial use. Table 9.40 shows six observations from lougharn lexicon.

We need to install textdata package to access ‘afinn’, ‘nrc’, and ‘loughran’ lexicon. The get_sentiments() function internally uses textdata::lexicon_afinn(), tex-tdata::lexicon nrc(), textdata::lexicon loughran() to download these lexicons and make it available for use. All the above lexicons were constructed and validated by the authors of the lexicons, using crowd-sourcing platforms. The advantage of using these lexicons is that we can quickly arrive at the sentiments from a corpus. The disadvantage is that the accuracy of the sentiments may be questionable if the style of writing in a corpus is very different (say, a book which is 100 years old and we use the above lexicon to decide on the sentiments being expressed in the book).

9.9 | Sentiment Analysis with Negative Words

In the previous section, we arrived at the sentiment by counting the positive and negative words. However, one of the drawbacks of counting single words is that words on their own may not convey a positive or negative emotion.

1. I am not happy – This sentence may convey a positive emotion if we look at the words in unigram fashion. However, ‘not happy’ means a negative emotion.

One of the ways to deal with such sentiments is to look at the n-gram (bigrams/tri-grams) to arrive at the sentiment score. We already created bigrams (‘separated_bigram’ variable) in Section 9.7.6. Let us look at all the words which were preceded by ‘not.

From Table 9.53, we can see that the most common words used with not were ‘discriminate’, ‘over’, ‘forget, ‘attend, etc. We also see that there are stop_words (like, to, a, etc.) appearing in the table but which do not convey an emotion. Let us use the AFINN lexicon to identify words preceded with negation words (‘not, ‘no, ‘never, ‘without, ‘dont’) and conveying emotion. Table 9.54 shows the words and the sentiment score. Of course, these sentiment scores need to be interpreted in contrary. A negative score denotes a positive sentiment and a positive score denotes a negative sentiment.

From Table 9.54, we see that the most common word associated with not was forget, which actually should have a score of +1 (as it is preceded by ‘not’). We can calculate how much a word has contributed in the wrong direction. We will multiply ‘value’ and ‘n’ columns in Table 9.54 to get the contribution. Contribution intuitively suggests that a word with a value of say +2 occurring five times has as much impact as a word with a sentiment value of + 1 occurring 10 times. Table 9.55 shows the contribution of each word.

9.10 | | Document Term Matrix

In all the previous sections, we processed and arranged text in a tabular format such that it was ‘one token per document (tweets by a user/screenName here) per row’. The benefit of doing so was a quick summarization and visualization of text data as well as in sentiment analysis. However, this tabular structure of data may not be compatible with packages which apply other NLP models on the data.

One of the most common structures text mining packages work with is the document-term matrix (or DTM). DTM matrix has the following structure (Silge and Robinson, 2017):

1. Each row represents one document (such as tweet by the user/screenName).

2. Each column represents one token (unigram/bigram, etc.).

3. Each value (typically) contains the number of appearances of that term in that document.

This structure is exactly the same as in Tables 9.5 and 9.6 from Section 9.6.1. Intuitively, we can visualize that DTM will be a sparse matrix, that is, most pairings of document and word will have a value of zero. However, DTMs are created in efficient ways by different packages. The cast() from tidytext package can be used to convert a tabular data from previous sections in a DTM format. Tidytext provides three variations of cast function:

1. cast_sparse() – converts to a sparse matrix which can be used with Matrix package.

2. cast_dtm() – converts to DTM object to be used in operations from tm package.

3. cast_dfm() – converts to a Document Feature Matrix (DFM) object which can work with quanteda package. DFM is just another name for DTM.

Given a DTM, tidytext also provides tidy() function which will convert the DTM to a tabular format (one token per document per row) for easy summarization and visualization of data.

We will use the cast() to create a DTM and merge it with the original tweet data-frame, that is, covid_twitter_df. Before we create the DTM and merge, a few things to keep in mind are as follows:

1. We will create twitter_word dataframe as done in Section 9.7.2. However, it will be without deleting the retweets while performing the text preprocessing.

2. Rather than using the screenName as a synonym to document ID, we will create a doc_id to keep track of the individual tweets.

Treating screenName as document ID in all the previous sections was not an issue since we wanted to summarize, visualize and do sentiment analysis for the users, that is, at screenName level. Let us understand why the second point becomes important from a DTM perspective. The covid_twitter_df is shown in Table 9.56.

From Table 9.56, we see that there are two tweets by screenName ‘MoHFW_INDIA’. If we use screenName as document ID, then while creating a DTM, the texts corresponding to both tweets will be shown in one document id itself. Since the idea is to merge the DTM back with the covid_twitter_df, we will want to treat these two tweets as two different documents. Thus, the reason for creating a new indicator called doc_id. Document Term Matrix acts as an input to several modelling techniques. Rather than merging the ‘tweet_dtm’, which is a DTM, with the original dataframe, we can use DTM as an input to Topic Modelling.

9.11 | | Topic Modelling

Topic modelling is an unsupervised learning algorithm which tries to extract the topics being discussed in a corpus. It treats

1. Every document as a mixture of topic.

2. Every topic as a mixture of words.

The number of topics to extract (k) from a document is a user-defined input to the topic modelling algorithm. Let us quickly apply the LDA() function from topicmodels package on the tweet_dtm DTM.

We can extract the per topic per word probability by using a parameter called beta in tidy(). Table 9.63 shows the probability of each word coming from the six topics.

We can visualize the top 10 words as a part of the six topics.

From Figure 9.24, we see the top words being used in each of the topics.

1. Words in topic 1 seem to suggest government rules and guidelines.

2. Words in topic 2 seem to suggest self-hygiene to be maintained.

3. Words in topic 3 seem to be talking about post-recovery support and symptoms.

4. Words (like festive, events, season, entertainment) in topic 4 seem to be talking about spreading awareness during festivals, etc.

Let us calculate the per document per topic probabilities by passing parameter ‘gamma’ to tidy().

From Table 9.64, we can see document topic probabilities for all documents. If a document shows a probability of 0.166 for all topics, that would mean the word used in that document does not emerge from that document. From Table 9.64, we clearly see that document 10 has 93% of the words belonging to topic 1. We can filter the covid_documents and understand the topics for each document. Table 9.65 shows the topics in document 1 and it seems document 1 mostly belongs to topic 4, that is, personal hygiene.

We briefly discussed topic model in this section. Topic models may become much more useful to apply in documents where the length of the document is not restricted like in tweets. There are other visualization charts which can be prepared from the topic models. We leave it for the readers to try out different visualizations on the topic models.

Summary

In this chapter, we learnt

1. Setting up a system to scrap twitter data and the importance of regular expressions in text preprocessing.

2. Text is unstructured data and needs extensive preprocessing before visualization and sentiment analysis. Regular expressions are helpful in text preprocessing.

3. Documents or sentences can be tokenized into unigrams or n-grams for building features.

4. Documents can be represented as vectors with words or n-grams as features. The vectors can be created using simple counts, TF (Term Frequency), or TF-IDF values.

5. A robust set of features can be created by removing stop words and applying stemming or lemmatization. The number of features can also be limited by selecting only features with higher frequencies.

6. Inbuilt lexicons such as afinn, nrc, bing, etc., can be used to understand the emotions of a text data. Visualization of unigrams and bigrams may help in getting a contextual understanding of the data.

7. Document Term Matrix becomes an input to several modelling techniques. We understood the use of DTM in the context of topic models.
